title: Connect a robot's sensor cable: hold the loose proximity sensor still while turning the M12 coupling ring tight
instruction: Connect the robot's sensor cable to the new proximity sensor: pull the red protective cap off the sensor's connector and drop it in the blue parts tray; take the cable's connector off its parking holder and push it onto the sensor's connector; the sensor turns in its bracket because its nuts are not tightened yet, so hold the sensor still with one hand while the other turns the connector's knurled coupling ring until it is tight and the sensor's green light comes on. Then let go of both and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Robot cells are wired with M12 screw connectors; a technician connecting a newly fitted sensor holds the sensor still, because the coupling ring's thread drags a sensor whose mounting nuts are still loose round with it.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) An aluminium fixture plate 1 cm thick, from 19 to 55 cm forward and from 20 cm right to 12 cm left of the centre line, fixed. (2) On it an anodised aluminium angle bracket whose 6 mm plate (5 cm wide) holds the sensor, fixed. (3) A steel inductive proximity sensor (0.13 kg): an M30 threaded stainless-steel barrel 3 cm across and 7 cm long with an orange plastic sensing face, two nickel-plated jam nuts (34 mm across flats) either side of the bracket's plate, and a grey plastic back end with a power light ring and a brass M12 male connector; its axis points 30 degrees down and to the left, at a machined aluminium part (5 x 4 x 3 cm, 0.15 kg, loose) in a blue nest at 30 cm forward, 8 cm left; its back end's face is 30 cm forward, 3 cm right of the centre line and 10.5 cm above the table. The jam nuts are loose: the sensor turns freely about its axis in the bracket. (4) A red rubber protective cap (1.9 cm across, 1.4 cm long, 8 g) on the sensor's connector. (5) The robot's orange PUR sensor cable, 5.5 mm thick, coming out of a grey cable duct (33 to 55 cm forward, 15 cm right, fixed) and ending, 19 cm on, in an M12 connector (28 g): a black moulded body 1.6 cm across with a knurled nickel-plated brass coupling ring 2.1 cm across and 1.6 cm long. It is parked on a black parking receptacle with a dummy thread, on a post at 23.5 cm forward, 3 cm right, at the same height and angle as the sensor. (6) A blue plastic parts tray, 6 cm square inside and 1.8 cm deep, at 24 cm forward, 12.5 cm right, fixed. (7) An orange robot arm parked behind the station (its base 66 cm forward, 15 cm right), fixed. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end. The connector is on (its thread has caught) once its front sits within 4 mm of the sensor's back end along the axis, within 3 mm of the axis and within 15 degrees of it; from then on it stays on the sensor's axis. While it is on, only the coupling ring's turn against the sensor (clockwise seen from behind) screws it on; the ring drags a sensor nobody holds round with it (a spring toward the ring's turn, at most 5 degrees behind). It is tight after one full turn against the sensor, and then the sensor's green light comes on; turned back 0.6 turns, it comes off. 1.0: the cap lies in the blue tray, the connector is on and tight, both hands have let go (each gripper's fingertip centre at least 4 cm from the coupling ring and from where the barrel is held) and both arms are back where they started (each within 5 cm); 0.5: the connector is on and tight; 0.25: the connector is on; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the connector, sensor and cap still.
reset_notes: Unscrew the connector and park it on its parking receptacle, put the red cap back on the sensor's connector, and turn the sensor back so its yellow light faces up.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the thread's friction on a loose sensor is a spring (at most 0.03 N m) turning the sensor with the ring; once on, a joint keeps the connector on the axis; one turn makes it tight (a real M12 takes about four); the moulded body turns with the ring. The cable is three stiff segments on damped ball joints. The plate, bracket, receptacle, duct, tray and robot are fixed. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
